modes.label: Building a foundation
modes.description: Choose a focused, familiar task. Plan support that helps you understand and share meaning.

modes.label: Extending what you can do
modes.description: Use connected ideas and plan ways to ask follow-up questions, add detail, or clarify meaning.

modes.label: Working more independently
modes.description: Plan a purposeful task for an audience or situation, with strategies for handling unfamiliar language.

feedback_guidance.source_document: Writing a good objective; ACTFL Proficiency Level Summary Descriptions
writing_criteria: Specific to a thematic context: the statement should relate directly to this week's topic and context, not be a generic language skill.
Appropriate for the proficiency level: language and demands should match what a Novice learner can reasonably do (see proficiency_notes).

Appropriate for the communicative mode: for interpretive modes it should name the type of text; for presentational modes it should name the audience or purpose; for interpersonal modes it should name the other person and how the exchange continues.
Measurable: it clearly defines an outcome that is observable, not a vague skill like 'talk about X'.
Identifies the communicative function: uses a specific verb such as describe, compare, ask, explain, recommend, or exchange rather than a vague verb like talk or learn.
Provides a real-world context: the language use is connected to an authentic situation with a real purpose, not just a classroom exercise.
checklist: Is it connected to the theme of this week's plan?
Does it match a Novice proficiency level?
Does it fit the communicative mode it's written for?
Is it something someone could actually observe the student doing?
Does it use a specific communicative function (describe, compare, ask, explain, recommend, persuade, etc.) rather than a vague verb like talk or learn?
Does it happen in a realistic situation for a real purpose?
feedback_guidance.common_pitfall: The most frequent weak statement is a generic skill with no function or context, e.g. 'I can talk about food' or 'I can learn food vocabulary' — missing both a specific communicative function and a real-world purpose. Compare: 'I can order a meal at a restaurant, ask questions about the menu, and explain my food preferences.'

target_level_descriptions.Novice Low: Can produce isolated words or memorized chunks with significant pauses and repetition. Communication is limited to lists or single, rehearsed phrases. Relies heavily on listeners to interpret meaning.
target_level_descriptions.Novice Mid: Can handle simple exchanges using memorized phrases and familiar topics. Responses are short, often formulaic. Speech reflects survival-type communication (e.g., greetings, ordering food).
target_level_descriptions.Novice High: Can manage short, simple conversations in predictable contexts. Begins to recombine memorized phrases into new sentences. Breaks down when asked to narrate, describe in detail, or handle unexpected situations.

proficiency_notes.above_target_note: Statements that require narrating in paragraphs, handling complications, discussing abstract topics, or sustaining unscripted conversation describe Intermediate-level ability or higher. Flag these as more ambitious than this course expects, not simply as 'too hard' — the student should scale the statement down to something observable at the Novice level instead.

areas.label: Interpersonal listening and speaking
areas.description: Exchange meaning with another person by listening, responding, and helping the interaction continue.
areas.learner_friendly_definition: Interpersonal speaking is the skill of communicating with another person through a two-way conversation by asking questions, answering, and negotiating meaning.
novice_examples: Introduce yourself and ask someone's name.
Order food and answer simple follow-up questions.
Make plans with a friend by discussing where and when to meet.
Ask for help in a store and explain what you are looking for.
strong_examples: I can ask and answer questions about weekend plans with a partner and ask one follow-up question.
I can discuss a favorite meal with a classmate and respond to one question about it.
self_checks: Does it name an exchange with another person?
Can someone hear or observe the interaction?
Is the topic and action focused enough for this week?
areas.source_document: FILL and ACTFL-aligned planning guidance; Communicative Modes descriptions

areas.label: Interpretive: Reading
areas.description: Make meaning from written language by identifying a message, details, or useful patterns.
areas.learner_friendly_definition: Interpretive reading is the skill of making meaning from written texts by using language you know and clues from the text, even when you don't understand every word.
novice_examples: Read a café menu and choose a meal.
Read a classroom schedule to find your next class.
Read a short email to understand what someone is asking you to do.
Read an online event announcement and determine when, where, and what is happening.
strong_examples: I can read a short event listing and identify the main idea and two details I would use.
I can read a restaurant menu and identify three items that fit a planned meal.
self_checks: Does it say what I will understand or identify?
Is the text type or purpose clear?
Could I show notes or a brief explanation as evidence?
areas.source_document: FILL and ACTFL-aligned planning guidance; Communicative Modes descriptions

areas.label: Interpretive: Listening
areas.description: Make meaning from spoken language by listening for a message, details, or familiar patterns.
areas.learner_friendly_definition: Interpretive listening is the skill of making meaning from spoken language by using words you recognize, context, and other clues, even when you don't understand every word.
novice_examples: Listen to someone introduce themselves and identify their name.
Follow simple classroom directions from your teacher.
Listen to a voicemail and identify the reason for the call.
Listen to a conversation between friends and determine their plans for the weekend.
strong_examples: I can listen to a short weather report and identify the forecast and two details.
I can listen to a brief announcement and note when and where the event happens.
weak_examples: I can listen to a podcast.
self_checks: Does it focus on meaning rather than just listening time?
Does it name what I will identify or understand?
Is the audio manageable for this week?
areas.source_document: FILL and ACTFL-aligned planning guidance; Communicative Modes descriptions

areas.label: Interpretive: Viewing
areas.description: Make meaning from a visual or audiovisual text using what you see and hear.
areas.learner_friendly_definition: Interpretive viewing is the skill of making meaning from visual and audiovisual texts by using language you know, images, context, and other clues, even when you don't understand everything.
novice_examples: Watch a short video and identify the setting and people.
Interpret a map or transit diagram to find a destination.
Watch a cooking demonstration and identify the sequence of steps.
Watch a travel video and identify activities, places, and cultural practices being highlighted.
strong_examples: I can watch a short cooking clip and explain the sequence of three actions I notice.
I can view a short tour and identify three details about the location.
self_checks: Does it identify a visible or audible meaning task?
Does it name what I will explain or notice?
Can I save notes or a response as evidence?
areas.source_document: FILL and ACTFL-aligned planning guidance; Communicative Modes descriptions

areas.label: Interpersonal writing
areas.description: Exchange meaning in writing by responding to another person and sustaining a brief interaction.
areas.learner_friendly_definition: Interpersonal writing is the skill of communicating with another person through written exchanges by asking questions, sharing information, and responding to messages.
novice_examples: Send a text asking what time to meet.
Reply to a message confirming plans.
Write an email asking for information about an event or activity.
Exchange messages with a language partner about hobbies or daily routines.
strong_examples: I can exchange three short messages about a meal plan and respond with one question.
I can reply to a classmate's message about weekend plans and ask a follow-up question.
self_checks: Does it include another person’s message or response?
Does it explain how the exchange will continue?
Is it a writing interaction, not a one-way composition?
areas.source_document: FILL and ACTFL-aligned planning guidance; Communicative Modes descriptions

areas.label: Presentational speaking
areas.description: Prepare spoken language to share information, ideas, or reactions with an audience.
areas.learner_friendly_definition: Presentational speaking is the skill of organizing and sharing ideas, information, or opinions with an audience through spoken language without immediate interaction.
novice_examples: Introduce yourself to the class.
Describe your family using simple sentences.
Talk about your favorite food or hobby.
Give a short presentation about your daily routine.
strong_examples: I can give a one-minute spoken recommendation for a local place and include two reasons.
I can record a short description of my dorm room for a new student.
weak_examples: I can talk about my topic.
I can speak for one minute.
self_checks: Does it name what I will communicate?
Is the audience or purpose apparent?
Could I record or perform it as evidence?
areas.source_document: FILL and ACTFL-aligned planning guidance; Communicative Modes descriptions

areas.label: Presentational writing
areas.description: Prepare writing to share information, ideas, or reactions with an audience.
areas.learner_friendly_definition: Presentational writing is the skill of organizing and sharing ideas, information, or opinions in writing for an audience without expecting an immediate response.
novice_examples: Write a short paragraph introducing yourself.
Create a simple postcard describing a place you visited.
Write a few sentences about your favorite animal.
Make a labeled poster about your school or community.
strong_examples: I can write a short post describing a favorite activity and give two supporting details.
I can write a brief recommendation for a campus event with a clear audience in mind.
self_checks: Does it name a clear written message?
Does it have a purpose or audience?
Is the amount of writing achievable this week?
areas.source_document: FILL and ACTFL-aligned planning guidance; Communicative Modes descriptions

areas.label: Intercultural competence
areas.description: Notice, investigate, and explain perspectives, practices, or products in context without assuming one experience represents everyone.
areas.learner_friendly_definition: Intercultural communicative competence is the ability to interact with people from other cultures with curiosity, respect, and an openness to understanding different perspectives and practices.
novice_examples: Learn and use appropriate greetings or gestures in another culture.
Notice similarities and differences between your daily routines and those of people in another culture.
Ask respectful questions to better understand another person's traditions or point of view.
Reflect on how cultural perspectives influence communication and adapt your language or behavior appropriately.
strong_examples: I can compare how two event invitations show expectations for guests and explain one question I still have.
I can examine a food-related post and identify one practice it shows and one question to investigate.
self_checks: Does it focus on context and evidence, not a stereotype?
Does it name what I will compare, notice, or investigate?
Does it leave room for curiosity or further questions?
areas.source_document: FILL and ACTFL-aligned planning guidance; Communicative Modes descriptions

learning_plan_intro: To work toward your Weekly Can-Dos, think about three types of learning activities during the week.

learning_plan_stages.title: Input — Finding Language to Learn From
learning_plan_stages.description: Input activities help you discover how people use the language you need. You find examples of real language, notice useful words and expressions, and discover the language bits you need to communicate your message.
activities: Watch videos, movies, shows, or social media clips related to your topic.
Listen to podcasts, interviews, conversations, or songs.
Read websites, articles, menus, advertisements, blogs, or messages.
Explore authentic materials from places where the language is spoken.
Notice useful vocabulary, phrases, and sentence patterns.
Look for explanations or examples of grammar and language structures you need in instructional materials.
Create a collection of useful words and expressions.
Compare how ideas are expressed in your language and the target language.
learning_plan_stages.brainstorm_prompt: What are some ways I could find input of the language I need to make progress on my Can-Dos?
learning_plan_stages.field_prompt: For Input, list two or three activities you can do this week that can help you with your can-do goal
learning_plan_stages.source_section_or_page: Can-do feedback / weekly planning training documentation

learning_plan_stages.title: Interaction and Practice — Using Language to Communicate
learning_plan_stages.description: Interaction activities give you opportunities to use the language you are learning to exchange messages with other people. The goal is to communicate meaning, ask questions, respond, and keep communication going.
activities: Have a conversation with a classmate, tutor, teacher, or language partner.
Use the Speakology conversation practice.
Go to conversation tables.
Practice asking and answering questions about your topic out loud or in writing.
Exchange messages through text, email, or online discussion.
Role-play a real-world situation.
Interview someone about their experiences or opinions.
Describe, compare, explain, or share information with another person.
Practice using new vocabulary in complete messages or writing a dialogue.
Record yourself practicing a conversation and try again.
learning_plan_stages.brainstorm_prompt: What are some ways I could practice communicating to achieve my Weekly Can-Do?
learning_plan_stages.field_prompt: For Interaction and Practice, list two or three activities you can do this week that can help you with your can-do goal
learning_plan_stages.source_section_or_page: Can-do feedback / weekly planning training documentation

learning_plan_stages.title: Production — Creating Evidence of Learning
learning_plan_stages.description: Production activities allow you to show what you can do by creating a spoken, written, or multimedia product.
activities: Record a video or audio presentation.
Write a message, email, blog post, review, or description.
Create a poster, infographic, brochure, or guide.
Give a short presentation.
Create a recommendation, explanation, or comparison.
Share your opinion or perspective on a topic.
Screenshot your participation in an online conversation or app.
Create something that could be useful to another person.
learning_plan_stages.brainstorm_prompt: What could I create or present to show I can accomplish my Weekly Can-Do?
learning_plan_stages.field_prompt: For Production, list two or three activities you can do this week that can help you with your can-do goal
